title: Observability basics: logs, metrics, traces and alerts
objectives: Say which question a log, a metric and a trace each answer, and write structured log lines that carry the request's trace ID
Choose counter, gauge or histogram for a measurement, follow Prometheus naming, and keep label cardinality bounded
Read a trace — spans, parent/child, kind, status — and explain how `traceparent` carries it across services
Explain why an average hides tail latency, and compute percentiles and an under-300 ms share from cumulative `le` buckets
Alert on symptoms users feel — golden signals and error-budget burn rate — rather than on causes like CPU

sources.title: Google SRE book: Monitoring Distributed Systems
Google SRE workbook: Alerting on SLOs
Grafana docs: Dashboard best practices (RED, USE)

questions.prompt: Checkout's p99 jumped from 300 ms to 4 s ten minutes ago. What tells you **which downstream call** got slow?

options.text: A trace of a slow checkout — its spans show which hop took the time
The service's average latency graph
The latency histogram broken down by a `user_id` label
CPU utilisation on the database host

questions.explanation: The metric already told you *that* something is slow; a trace tells you *where*, because each hop — database query, payment call — is a timed span in one tree. The average is what hid the problem in the first place. A `user_id` label would explode the series count without saying anything about downstream calls. Database CPU is a possible cause to check once the trace points at the database.

questions.prompt: Which log line is most useful when you're debugging one failed order at 3 a.m.?

options.text: `{"level":"error","msg":"order failed","order_id":"o_123","duration_ms":2310,"trace_id":"c50e…"}`
`order o_123 failed after 2310ms: payment timeout`
The JSON of the whole incoming request, headers and body included
`console.log(err)` in the catch block

questions.explanation: Named fields can be filtered and aggregated without regex, and the `trace_id` joins the line to the request's trace and to every other line it wrote. The sentence has the facts but buried in prose. Logging whole requests copies `Authorization` headers, cookies and personal data into a system with wide access and long retention. A bare error has no order ID, no duration and no way to find the request it belonged to.

questions.prompt: Which metric type fits "jobs currently waiting in the queue"?

options.text: A gauge — a current value that goes up and down
A counter named `jobs_waiting_total`
A histogram of queue sizes
A summary with p50 and p99 quantiles

questions.explanation: Queue depth rises and falls, so it's a gauge (an `UpDownCounter` or `Gauge` in OpenTelemetry). Prometheus's docs: don't use a counter for a value that can decrease — a counter only grows, and you read it through `rate()`. A *counter* fits "jobs enqueued" (`jobs_enqueued_total`); a histogram fits "how long jobs waited".

questions.prompt: Which label on `http_server_request_duration_seconds` would make the number of time series grow without bound?

options.text: `path="/orders/o_8f3k2"` — the raw request path
`route="/orders/:id"` — the route template
`method="GET"`
`status="200"`

questions.explanation: Every distinct label combination is a separate time series, and a raw path has one value per order — unbounded, multiplied by every bucket of the histogram. The route template has one value per endpoint, and method and status have a handful each. OpenTelemetry's HTTP conventions require `http.route` to be low-cardinality for this reason; per-request detail like the order ID belongs on spans and logs.

questions.prompt: Service A calls service B over HTTP, but B's spans always start a **new** trace instead of joining A's. What's the most likely cause?

options.text: The `traceparent` header isn't sent — e.g. a hand-rolled HTTP client with no instrumentation injecting it
Clock skew between the two hosts
B's spans use kind `INTERNAL` instead of `SERVER`
A sets its spans' status to `OK`

questions.explanation: Context crosses a process boundary only in the request: the W3C `traceparent` header carries the trace ID and the caller's span ID, and B's server span adopts them. No header, no link — B starts a fresh trace. Clock skew distorts timings, not trace IDs; span kind and status don't decide which trace a span joins.

questions.prompt: Two instances serve equal traffic. One reports p99 = 1,000 ms, the other p99 = 10 ms. What is the service's p99?

options.text: Can't be computed from those two numbers — aggregate the histogram buckets across instances, then take the quantile
505 ms, the average of the two
1,000 ms, the worse of the two
10 ms, because most traffic is fast

questions.explanation: Percentiles don't average. If every request took 10 ms except two 1-second ones on the first instance, the true p99 of all 200 requests is 10 ms, and the average, 505 ms, is a latency no request had — Prometheus calls averaged quantiles "statistically nonsensical". Histogram buckets are counters, so they *can* be summed across instances (`sum by (le) (rate(...))`) before `histogram_quantile`; precomputed summary quantiles can't.

questions.prompt: The objective is "99% of requests within 250 ms", but the histogram's bounds are 100, 300 and 1,000 ms. What can you compute exactly?

options.text: Nothing exact for 250 ms — add a 250 ms bucket bound, then it's `count(le=250) / count(+Inf)`
Use the `le="300"` bucket; it's close enough
Interpolate between the 100 and 300 ms buckets for the exact share
Check that `_sum / _count` is under 250 ms

questions.explanation: A cumulative bucket answers "how many took ≤ le" only for its own bound. The 300 ms bucket counts requests between 250 and 300 ms as passing, so it overstates compliance; interpolation is an estimate that assumes requests are spread evenly inside the bucket; the mean says nothing about the 99th percentile. Prometheus's guide notes the "within 300 ms" query strictly requires a boundary at 0.3 — so put bounds at your thresholds.

questions.prompt: Which of these should page someone at 3 a.m.?

options.text: Checkout errors burning the 30-day error budget at 14.4× for the last hour (2% of the budget gone), still high over the last 5 minutes
CPU above 90% on one node for 5 minutes
A disk at 80%, growing 1% a month
Any single HTTP 500

questions.explanation: That's a symptom users feel, significant (2% of the month's budget in an hour is the SRE workbook's suggested paging threshold) and still happening (the short window). High CPU is a possible cause that may hurt no one; the disk needs a ticket, not a wake-up; a single 500 is noise against any realistic budget. The SRE book's test: every page should be actionable and require intelligence to handle.

questions.prompt: Why does the SRE workbook advise against paging on "error rate above the SLO's 0.1% for 10 minutes"?

options.text: Such a blip spends only about 0.02% of a 30-day budget, so it pages people for something that barely matters
Ten minutes is too slow; it should page on the first error over 0.1%
Error rate is a cause, not a symptom
Short windows create too many time series

questions.explanation: The workbook's example: a 0.1% error rate for 10 minutes would alert while consuming only 0.02% of the monthly error budget. Burn-rate alerts instead ask how fast the budget is going — 14.4× over an hour, confirmed by a 5-minute window, pages; a slow burn of 1× over three days opens a ticket. Error rate is very much a symptom; the problem is the threshold and window, not the signal.

prompts.prompt: Put the active span's trace ID on a structured log line (OpenTelemetry JS API).
code: logger.info({ msg: "order placed", order_id: orderId, trace_id: ctx?.___ });
prompts.explanation: A span's context carries `traceId` and `spanId`. Putting the trace ID on every log line links logs to traces across services; OpenTelemetry's log bridges can add it automatically when your logging library is routed through the SDK.

prompts.prompt: Requests per second over the last 5 minutes, from a counter.
prompts.explanation: A counter's raw value only grows and resets on restart, so it's never graphed directly. `rate()` gives the per-second increase over the window and adjusts for resets — take the rate first, then `sum` across instances, or resets go undetected.

prompts.prompt: Share of requests that finished within 300 ms, from a classic histogram in seconds.
prompts.explanation: `le` means "less than or equal": the 0.3 bucket counts every request of 300 ms or less, because buckets are cumulative. Dividing by `_count` (equal to the `+Inf` bucket) gives the share. It only works if 0.3 is an actual bucket bound — Prometheus won't invent one.

prompts.prompt: Mark the span as failed — not just annotated — and make sure it's exported.
prompts.explanation: `recordException` only adds an `exception` event; the span's status stays `UNSET` ("no error") until you call `setStatus` with `ERROR`, which is what error-rate views count. `end()` in `finally` runs on both paths — a span that's never ended is never exported.

prompts.prompt: The W3C Trace Context header that carries a trace into the next service.
prompts.explanation: `traceparent` is `version-traceid-parentid-flags`: here version `00`, a 32-hex-digit trace ID, the caller's 16-hex-digit span ID, and flags `01` (sampled). OpenTelemetry's default propagator reads and writes it; HTTP instrumentation does that for you, hand-written clients have to.

snippets.question: What does it print?
snippets.explanation: Without a comparator, `sort()` converts values to strings and compares them character by character: "1200" < "300" < "40" < "5". A percentile helper built on it returns 300 as the median of these four. Use `sort((a, b) => a - b)` — on a copy (`[...xs]`), because `sort` also reorders the caller's array.

code: const mean = samples.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / samples.length;
snippets.question: What are the mean, p95 and p99?
snippets.explanation: The mean, 49.8 ms, matches no request anyone made and barely moves when the slow ones get slower. p95 is still 10 ms because only 2% of requests are slow; p99 lands on them. Report percentiles, and watch the tail.

code: // The exported span's status code: UNSET = 0, OK = 1, ERROR = 2
snippets.question: What status does the exported `charge-card` span have?
acceptable: unset — it counts as a success
snippets.explanation: `recordException` attaches an `exception` event and nothing else; the status stays at its default, `UNSET`, which means "completed without error". An error-rate view built on span status counts this declined card as a success. Call `span.setStatus({ code: SpanStatusCode.ERROR })` as well — OpenTelemetry's docs recommend doing both. (Run with `@opentelemetry/sdk-trace-node` 2.11.)

code: // Top-level code: no span is active yet.
snippets.question: Is `query-db` a child of `load-order` in the exported trace?
snippets.answer: No — it has no parent and starts its own trace
acceptable: no, it's a separate root span
snippets.explanation: `startSpan` creates a span without making it the active one, so the next span is started from whatever context was active before — here, none — and becomes a root in a new trace. Use `startActiveSpan(name, (span) => { … })` to make spans inside the callback its children, or pass a context explicitly.
